current_answer: Norwegian employer-register data through July 2026 do not show a clear employment split between the most and least AI-exposed occupations overall: the private-sector gap is +1.5 percentage points for ages 21–60 (standard error 2.7), and −0.8 points for ages 21–30 (standard error 4.0), since the pre-ChatGPT baseline. This is exposure, not observed employer AI adoption, and it cannot isolate an AI effect. A Spanish occupation study finds a small rise in registered-unemployment counts with exposure but no persistent new-contract decline; that too is noncausal. U.S. young-worker payroll data show a sharper warning in a selected panel, while Yale’s broad U.S. tracker sees no clear economy-wide footprint. Different countries, populations and outcomes do not yield one job-loss count or a personal forecast.

catalogue_card.question: Are exposed jobs shrinking in Norway?
catalogue_card.text: A national payroll index finds no clear employment gap between the most and least AI-exposed occupations overall. Its younger-worker comparison is uncertain; neither result proves what AI caused.

summary: Norwegian employer-register data through July 2026 show an imprecise +1.5-point employment gap between most and least exposed private-sector occupations across ages 21–60; ages 21–30 show −0.8 points since the pre-ChatGPT baseline.

A Spanish occupation-level study finds a small rise in registered unemployment where AI exposure is higher, but no persistent fall in new contracts. The comparison does not show that employer AI use caused job loss.
A separate Spanish analysis finds employment growth in all exposure groups through 2025; it uses a different measure and outcome, so it does not directly refute the unemployment finding.
A revised seven-country survey of nearly 9,000 senior executives reports little net firm-employment impact attributed to AI so far; more than 40% forecast a positive or negative effect at their firm.
Pew finds slower U.S. employment growth for women than men in more AI-exposed occupations, concentrated among workers without bachelor’s degrees; the comparison is not causal.
Newly classified duties in U.S. job ads increased in high-AI-use occupations, but a duty statement is not a completed hire or a new job.

A randomized hiring-vignette study found that framing student AI use as replacing learning lowered stated interview and salary-negotiation ratings for fictional U.S. graduates; it did not observe real hiring.
The September Stanford–ADP payroll update shows a year-over-year employment decline of 3.7% among ages 22–25 in high-AI-exposure occupations versus 0.2% growth in the least-exposed.
The same high-versus-low comparison is −2.8% versus +0.9% for ages 26–30, and −0.5% versus +1.0% across all ages.
uncertainty: The Norwegian October dashboard is a descriptive register series through July 2026, not a causal study of employer AI adoption; its exposure-gap standard errors are large, and the 21–30 group may conceal narrower 22–25 changes.

Spain’s new gradient uses registered-unemployment counts, not unemployment rates; the full pre-treatment test rejects, the later estimate is imprecise, and the exposure score is not observed Spanish employer use.

The revised seven-country firm survey relies on senior executives’ own reports of AI’s past effects and their expectations for the next three years. Its abstract reports a near-zero aggregate net effect, which can conceal firm-level gains and losses; the full revised paper was not accessible through the browser.

The Canaries September update uses a selected ADP firm panel, excludes firm entry and exit, and groups occupations by exposure rather than actual AI use; it is descriptive, not nationally representative or causal.

Germany’s full-time employee analysis ends in 2025, excludes several worker groups and uses occupation potential rather than actual AI adoption; its adjusted young-worker exposure estimate is not statistically significant.
The remote-work study is observational and ends in 2025; it cannot rule out later or country-specific AI effects.
The French analysis is descriptive and its flows do not measure age-by-occupation employment stocks.
Anthropic is one rapidly growing firm reporting internal, non-audited records.
The Copilot studies use different firm samples and hiring denominators; neither establishes an economy-wide effect.
The adaptive-capacity study combines occupation-level exposure and transition proxies, not observed AI layoffs or realized reemployment.
Occupation averages conceal individual circumstances; future demand may change the ranking.
A new German journal abstract covers mostly pre-generative-AI adoption; its full methods were not accessible.
The sector study uses task exposure rather than observed AI deployment and adjusts a pre-trend in its automatable-task series.
The Argentine experiment took place outside workplaces and did not test actual job access or wages.
The Swedish AI-skill study covers 2014–2023 external hires and excludes ordinary chatbot use; its observational pay gap cannot identify a causal return to training.
The October tracker summary did not expose its full updated data vintage or detailed estimates in the page inspected.
The new hiring-vignette finding concerns opt-in professionals’ hypothetical ratings, not actual callbacks, pay or student AI use.
Only the October new-duty paper’s abstract was accessible; the full classifier tests and sampling detail were not verified, and postings do not show realized work or pay.
Pew’s pre/post CPS comparison uses occupational task exposure, not employer AI adoption, and may reflect other changes.
freshness_note: Checked 31 October 2026. Norwegian employer registers show no clear broad exposure-linked employment decline through July; the younger subgroup remains uncertain.
